title: Science Desk Fall Relaunch: Events in New York and Chicago, and More
summary: Now more than ever, The New York Times is the place to learn about the world of science. This fall, the Science desk is relaunching its coverage — with new beats and columns…
body_markdown:
The Science desk is holding events at the American Museum of Natural History and the Griffith Museum of Science and Industry. Read more from Bill Wasik, Science editor.


Now more than ever, The New York Times is the place to learn about the world of science. This fall, the Science desk is[relaunching its coverage](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/15/insider/science-desk.html) — with new beats and columns, a redesigned newsletter and more — and in honor of that, we are putting on two events, in New York and Chicago.


On the evening of Wednesday, Oct. 28, we’ll be at the American Museum of Natural History on the Upper West Side of New York for an event called “The Future of Discovery: Science Times at the American Museum of Natural History.” It will feature panels about the past, present and future of space exploration, recent revolutions in cancer treatment, and some surprising questions about dinosaurs.


Guests will include **Jeremy Hansen** , one of the Artemis II astronauts; **Neil deGrasse Tyson** and **Roger Benson** from the museum; and **Carl Zimmer** and **Victoria Jaggard** from the Times Science desk. You’ll also hear from **Sean Decatur,** the museum’s president, as well as from me, the Times’s new science editor.


Click[here](https://www.amnh.org/onsite/science-times-amnh) to learn more on the museum’s website.


Then, on Sunday, Nov. 1, we’re hosting an event at the Griffith Museum of Science and Industry in Chicago. **Wendy Freedman** , a University of Chicago cosmologist who has done pathbreaking work on the expansion of the universe, will be in conversation with **Katrina Miller,** a Chicago-based space and physics reporter for The Times. The Science desk’s photography editor and another Chicagoan, **Matt McCann** , will deliver a presentation about the art of science imagery. Access is free with museum admission.


The best place to catch The Times’s expanded science coverage is our free Science Times newsletter, which we’ve revamped, redesigned and expanded with the science lovers in mind. If you aren’t a subscriber to the newsletter yet, please consider[signing up](https://www.nytimes.com/newsletters/science-times) today.
